name: bpm-tools
desc: Detect tempo of audio files using beats-per-minute (BPM)
why: Estimates tempo from audio files with a small, old-school signal processing idea behind it.

brief.what_it_is: bpm-tools is a small set of command-line programs that estimate the tempo, in beats per minute, of audio music files. The homepage describes the code as the best explanation of its algorithm, which is an autocorrelation applied by statistical sampling. The brew package installs two executables, bpm and bpm-tag. The homepage's scout note calls it an old-school signal processing approach. The homepage does not spell out the exact input formats or output format.
brief.why_it_exists: Mark Hills wrote it after experiments in automatically calculating and tagging the tempo of music files. It is aimed at DJs and at people who want tempo detection in scripts on the command line.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage describes the method as a relatively simple application of autocorrelation by statistical sampling. It gives no further detail, and points to the source code as the fullest explanation.

commands_seen.context: Clones the project's Git repository from the author's site. The homepage presents this as the way to get the source.

brief.install_notes: The homepage offers source via Git and names the most recent release as bpm-tools 0.3 from 21 May 2013. It gives no build steps, dependencies, or first-run instructions. The Git clone URL returned HTTP 403 when I tried it, so I could not read the repository or any README there.
brief.standout: The author says the code is its own best documentation, and the algorithm is a compact autocorrelation approach rather than a published, benchmarked method. It has been used with xwax, Mark Hills's Linux DJ software.
brief.status: Quiet. The most recent release named on the homepage is bpm-tools 0.3, dated 21 May 2013. The homepage itself was updated in December 2021. I found no commit history or release page to confirm activity after that.
brief.caveats: The homepage says there is no scientific comparison of the algorithm against other software. Licensing is GPLv2, which bars copying into proprietary software; commercial licences are available by contacting the author. The git clone endpoint returned 403. The homepage does not describe platforms beyond a mention of Linux and xwax use.
quotes: The code serves as the best explanation of the algorithm — a relatively simple application of an autocorrelation by statistical sampling.
As yet, there is no scientific comparison of the algorithm with others software.
It reliably detects the tempo of the vast majority of popular music I have used it with
